title: Camara on the ‘crazy’ achievement of joining Haas in 2027
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has a lot going for him. On track, he's killing it. The reigning F3 champion is currently leading the F2 championship with two rounds to go – and he was sensationally fast in Haas' shoot-out test.

Off track, he compartmentalises the fire and killer instinct needed to extract his racing potential and returns to being a kind, quietly-spoken, genuine 21-year-old.

We meet in a Central London hotel on the day he's announced as a Formula 1 driver. Like all of his soon to be rivals, it's a day that he's been dreaming about his whole life. And unsurprisingly, even though it has been some time since he's been told, it hasn't fully sunk in yet.

"It feels good," he says. "I'm very happy. It's something you've been working your whole life for this moment.

"It's just really crazy to achieve this. I'm just looking forward to start working with the team, to meet everyone in the factory and start as soon as possible."

Brazilian Camara entered the year knowing that if he delivered on his promise, Ferrari – whose junior programme he has been part of since 2021 – would almost certainly find a way to get him on the Formula 1 grid in 2027.

So, he got his head down and focused on trying to hit the ground running in F2 with Invicta Racing and put together a tilt at the title.

At times, a championship charge looked difficult – he was 47 points off the lead at one point – but he never panicked.

"I was just trying to make sure I did everything I could to make sure I would have no regrets this year," he continues. "So obviously I cannot be happier right now."

In a short space of time, he took the championship lead – and found out he would be driving for Haas next year. Alongside his F2 commitments, Ferrari also ploughed on preparing him for his arrival in F1 and that included a private test at the Hungaroring in Hungary in May.

A few months later, he found himself in Haas machinery taking part in an old-fashioned shoot-out test as Haas boss Ayao Komatsu evaluated four young drivers while he contemplated a replacement for Esteban Ocon. It was here that he solidified his chance to step up to F1.

Haas sign Ferrari junior Rafael Camara for 2027

"For sure it was an intense two days," says Camara of the test. "Obviously it was a new track, new team. I went to do the seat fit but obviously I didn't meet everyone, so it was a new environment and for sure it was quite intense.

"You have two days to make sure you are comfortable and you deliver what you need to deliver, and I was just a bit concerned about being a bit tight and not being myself. I just really wanted to make sure I was really enjoying because it was not going to be an opportunity that I would have again."

The Brazilian was able to calm those nerves and enjoy it to the extent that he was delivering lap times, in a range of tricky conditions, that made Komatsu and his engineering team take note. They were particularly impressed at how quickly he was able to extract performance out of the car – and adapt to the different conditions while keeping mistakes to a minimum.

I think I have always been able to extract the most of myself.Rafael Camara, F2 leader and future Haas driver

Those are traits that Camara has shown throughout his junior career. On his F3 debut in Melbourne, Australia, he posted the fastest lap on his second push lap in practice, despite never having driven the track before, and then went on to take pole. To be able to commit to a lap in reasonably unfamiliar machinery on a reasonably unfamiliar track was becoming his bread and butter.

"I think I have always been able to extract the most of myself," he says. "These days were really just trying to apply everything that I learned in the years in my single-seater career. Everything that I knew, it's just about putting it in place and making sure I was doing my job."

Camara has made the most of his opportunities. He admits that he was a "bit scared" when he joined the Ferrari junior programme and that he had to work hard to improve his English to in turn improve the way he communicated with the team.

But he threw himself into the challenge and, as a result, he feels like he was "able to learn a lot" and "to grow up not only as a driver but as a person as well" with Ferrari.

Having seen the likes of Charles Leclerc and Ollie Bearman progress from Ferrari juniors to Formula 1 drivers in recent times was also inspiring because he knew that, if he delivered on expectation, there was a strong chance he would get to follow in their footsteps.

Once Komatsu gave him the good news, he told his parents. "I didn't know how to say it to them so I just said quickly – I'll be driving next year," he says laughing. "My dad, he was more emotional. When he came to hug me, it was just... you cannot hold [the emotion], it just comes out."

When he arrives in Formula 1, he'll have some familiar faces around. He's known fellow Brazilian Gabriel Bortoleto since he was a kid, racing him in go-karts along with Kimi Antonelli, Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad.

Why Haas decided to risk promoting rookie Camara

"I have known Gabi since I was seven," he says. "We raced together in Brazil. Then in Europe he was always in the category above but we've always been together.

"We have been very close friends. To see him going [to F1]... for me it was another motivation to keep working and keep pushing so hopefully it would be two of us there – and it will be next year."

For now, though, Camara is resetting his focus to F2 and the final two rounds of the year. He leads Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov by seven points but if he can fend off the Bulgarian, he'll follow in the footsteps of the likes of Bortoleto, Oscar Piastri, George Russell and Leclerc in winning F3 and F2 back-to-back before ultimately making it into Formula 1.

"The aim is to finish on a high," he says. Once that's done and dusted he can switch his attention to the Haas project, with a run in the end-of-season young driver test planned ahead of an intense winter.

"There's a lot of things we need to speak about and organise," he says. "I'll just be waiting for them to tell me what to do – and I'll be ready."

title: Williams outline plans for 50th anniversary year in 2027
excerpt:
Williams have outlined plans for their 50th anniversary year in 2027, with a milestone chassis designation, an immersive experience in London and a fan-picked Silverstone car livery all set to feature throughout a calendar of special events.

Williams are set to become only the third F1 team, following on from rivals Ferrari and McLaren, to celebrate 50 continuous years in the sport, underlining their historic and storied status.

Described as the “centrepiece” of their celebrations, Williams will kick off 2027 with the ‘W50 Live’ experience in Waterloo, London – a theatrical, multi-sensory journey featuring title-winning cars and iconic memorabilia from the squad’s history.

It comes just over 50 years after Frank Williams discovered co-founder Patrick Head working in a garage under a London railway arch, marking the start of a journey that has led to nine Teams’ Championships, seven Drivers’ Championships and 114 Grand Prix victories.

Cars on display will include the FW06, which was the first chassis produced by Williams Grand Prix Engineering; the FW14B, which dominated the 1992 season and secured Nigel Mansell his crown; and the FW38, which still holds the record for the highest speed ever reached by an F1 car – 378kph by Valtteri Bottas at the 2016 Mexican Grand Prix.

‘W50 Live’ will also feature a show car of Williams’ 2027 challenger, which is to be named the FW50, moving straight from this year’s FW48, just as the team skipped from the FW38 to the FW40 on their 40th anniversary.

Other standout plans include giving fans the chance to choose their car livery for the British Grand Prix at Silverstone, which has played host to plenty of Williams milestones over the years – such as the team’s first F1 victory in 1979 with Clay Regazzoni, and their 100th race win with Jacques Villeneuve in 1997.

A series of limited-edition merchandise and collectible drops are also being worked on, all adorned with a commemorative W50 logo, with further anniversary moments to be revealed over the coming months.

“It is incredible to think that over 100 F1 teams have come and gone since Frank Williams built this team from next to nothing with a determination to race and win against motorsport’s powerhouses,” said Williams Team Principal James Vowles.

“That independence, passion and relentless will to win remain in our DNA as we enter our 50th year.

“Our celebrations will reintroduce the heroes and stories that have forged Williams’ legacy to a new generation of fans, who will carry us forward to reach new heights.”

Stefano Domenicali, F1 President and CEO, added: “It is incredible to celebrate 50 years of Williams in Formula 1.

“Sir Frank Williams built one of the defining teams in our sport, founded on determination, resilience and an uncompromising desire to succeed. Those values continue to inspire the team today as it writes the next chapter of its remarkable story.

“Williams is not only a vital part of our history, but of Formula 1’s identity, with achievements, memories and moments that will forever hold a special place in our sport.”

title: The next Ferrari protege Haas couldn’t turn down
excerpt:
Rafael Camara will step up to Formula 1 next season after impressing the Haas F1 Team enough to get the nod ahead of multiple other contenders.

The Brazilian has been part of Ferrari’s Driver Academy since 2022, when he was snapped up by the Scuderia much like current Haas driver Oliver Bearman.

Team Principal Ayao Komatsu was clear with what the team was looking for in their next driver: speed and a team-first mentality.

Based on Camara's career to date, and what has been said by those best-placed to assess his talents, it appears that Haas have picked the ideal candidate to complete their line-up for next season.

Speed

“You cannot teach them speed,” said Komatsu in Baku when discussing what Haas were looking for in their next driver, following the news that one-time race winner Esteban Ocon would be departing the US outfit at the end of the season.

“[They] need to be fast, but really [they] need to be a team player and especially for a small team like us.

"The two drivers, the integration into the team, how they motivate and drive the team, is very important.”

Haas sign Ferrari junior Rafael Camara for 2027

Renowned for his one-lap pace, Camara holds the record for most poles in a single FIA F3 season (five) and sits behind Charles Leclerc alone for most poles in a single F2 season, currently on five versus the Monegasque’s eight.

The Brazilian took part in a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) test for the American outfit and excited the team thoroughly with what he delivered.

Rivals for the seat included 2025 F2 Champion Leonardo Fornaroli, who is highly rated by McLaren, and Jack Doohan, who already has F1 experience under his belt. All told it was Camara that won over the team.

Team player

Earlier this season, and while he was still chasing his first victory in F2, Camara looked set to win around the streets of Monaco. An error whilst leading meant he had to wait.

One week on in Barcelona and Camara was at his very best. He was metronomic in pulling off an overcut strategy that required tyre conservation and consistent speed to leave his rivals well behind.

After the race, Camara’s Invicta Team Principal James Robinson paid tribute to the display, calling it “perfection” as he reflected on a great team effort.

“It was a really, really excellent strategy from him and his engineer and executed to perfection,” said Robinson. “I know there were a few comments on social media at the end of last week about the relationship between Rafa and his engineer.

“But I think that could not be more wrong in terms of the relationship there. Rafa, his engineer and the whole team have an absolutely magnificent relationship.

“Rafa's a brilliant part of the team. It’s great to finally convert the undoubted pace into a win and points. We feel very vindicated.”

Maturity

Driver confidence is crucial, as is quality of feedback. Komatsu said ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix that the team were working hard to provide their drivers with the best possible environment in which to succeed.

Jerome D’Ambrosio, Deputy Team Principal of Ferrari and the man overseeing the FDA, believes they are qualities Camara has in spades.

The Ferrari man revealed the extent of the Brazilian’s self-belief, as Camara took the initiative ahead of what turned out to be his most successful season to date.

ANALYSIS: Why Haas decided to risk promoting rookie Camara

“When you’ve got a talent like Rafa, this might sound harsh, but it is what you’re expecting and is what you want to see,” D’Ambrosio said last year.

“Our job is to support him in the best possible way so that he can deliver that and can express his talents to the maximum of its capacity.

“He has a unique way of knowing what he wants and what he needs to perform, which I think is extremely important for a driver.

“We had some discussions over the winter, which were quite interesting….as an academy, we were suggesting some things, and he said, ‘No, Jerome, this is what I need. This is what I want.’

“He knows what he wants or what he needs to perform, and that's a sign of maturity. That's a sign of strength.

“You have to know what you want, and you have to go for it. You have to believe in yourself, and you need to be objective by yourself also. Rafa has got these qualities.”

After winning the Formula Regional title in 2024, Camara has mirrored compatriot Gabriel Bortoleto’s success, winning the FIA Formula 3 title with TRIDENT. He currently heads the Formula 2 standings for Invicta with two rounds remaining.

Camara hasn’t finished lower than fifth in any series he’s entered and could become the first driver since Oscar Piastri to win three consecutive junior titles directly preceding F1 promotion.

He has consistently impressed those that work closely with him and has ticked all the boxes Haas set out. Next year he will set about impressing even more people with the way he operates in Formula 1.

title: Why Haas decided to risk promoting rookie Camara
excerpt:
There'll be a new face on the Formula 1 grid in 2027, with Haas signing promising talent and Brazilian F2 championship leader Rafael Camara.

Up until now, the Formula 1 driver market has been stable, with teams opting to renew drivers rather than switch things up.

However, it emerged after Baku that Haas would break with that strategy when the American team confirmed that one-time race winner Esteban Ocon would not get a third season.

With sophomore Ollie Bearman outperforming his team mate Ocon and some exciting young talent on the market, Team Principal Ayao Komatsu had decided to evaluate his options.

Utilising the Haas Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) programme, he ran the likes of F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, current championship leader Camara and Haas reserve drivers Ryo Hirakawa and Jack Doohan.

It is believed that very quickly during the test in Portimao, Portugal, Camara stood out.

The Brazilian has got better and better during his season with Invicta Racing in F2, culminating in him taking the championship lead with two race weekends to go.

When the 21-year-old got behind the wheel of F1 machinery, his speed and ability to adapt and get on the pace quickly instantly shone through.

Ferrari, who have been a partner of Haas since the American team joined the sport in 2016, also rate him highly, having evaluated him both on and off track through their junior programme.

Add into the mix that Camara, who is the reigning F3 champion, is a very attractive proposition from a commercial perspective and it's very easy to see why the Brazilian is such an attractive prospect.

Haas sign Ferrari junior Rafael Camara for 2027

It is a risk to promote a rookie, especially one who has yet to test current F1 machinery on a Grand Prix weekend, but Komatsu has taken confidence from successfully taking a chance on Bearman.

The Briton, who is also a Ferrari junior, has been stellar since joining Haas in 2025, with the American team showing they have what it takes to help a rising star move towards achieving their potential.

And so, with all that in mind, Haas decided to push ahead and sign Camara for next season, making him the second Brazilian on the grid alongside Gabriel Bortoleto.

Bearman favourite to retain his seat

There was no mention of who would be in the second seat at Haas, but sources say it will be Bearman.

The 21-year-old has levelled up in his second season with team, improving not only his single-lap pace but also his race craft.

He’s got a season’s best finish of fifth (in China) and has amassed 23 points to Ocon’s seven.

Komatsu is therefore keen to keep him and it is believed it is just a case of finalising a few small details before a new deal can be inked.

Ferrari are also understood to be happy with Bearman's progress at Haas and want him to continue there for now.

Sources say the Briton remains in contention for a step up to the famous Italian team in the future.

title: Haas sign Ferrari junior Rafael Camara for 2027
excerpt:
Formula 2 leader and Ferrari junior Rafael Camara will make the step up to Formula 1 for the 2027 season after signing a multi-year deal with American squad Haas.

The 21-year-old has competed in single-seaters since he first joined the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy in 2022, making his mark by winning the 2024 Formula Regional European Championship before he landed a Formula 3 seat for the following year.

There, Camara secured another title – equalling Arvid Lindblad for the highest win percentage in F3 history – and graduated to F2, in which he currently leads the drivers’ standings by seven points.

Three Feature Race victories and a further four podiums have given the Brazilian a seven-point advantage over Red Bull protege Nikola Tsolov in his rookie campaign, demonstrating the talent that has earned him a promotion to Haas.

He also showed his skill in an F1 car during a Testing of Previous Car (TPC) test in August, when he drove Haas' 2025 challenger at Portimao.

"I’m very happy to be joining TGR Haas F1 Team as a Formula 1 driver," said Camara. "It’s an important step in my career and I want to thank Gene Haas [team owner] and Ayao Komatsu [Haas Team Principal] for the trust they have placed in me.

"I’m also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey.

"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I’m looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."

ANALYSIS: Why Haas decided to risk promoting rookie Camara

Haas Team Principal Komatsu added: "I’m really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Camara. I don’t need to tell everyone about his achievements in the junior formulas, it’s been very impressive, and in his rookie season in Formula 2, the speed he’s shown in some very difficult moments, like qualifying in Monaco and Montreal – that all goes to show the potential Rafa has.

"He showed when we had him drive in our TPC program in Portugal that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed. Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special.

"We’re all excited about this opportunity and really committed as TGR Haas F1 Team to nurture this talent and provide a place where he can flourish. We want to create an environment where he’s comfortable and supported, where he can really excel in his capabilities."

Team owner Gene Haas commented: “I’m excited to see what Camara can achieve in Formula 1 having seen his accomplishments coming up through the ranks in Formula 3 and now Formula 2 this year.

"It’s a different challenge at this level but what we’ve experienced through Ollie Bearman following a similar trajectory and association with the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy, these younger drivers are well prepared, and they can make an immediate impact on a team.

"Rafa impressed the team with his TPC performance, so we look forward to building on that and growing our relationship full-time next season.”

The announcement follows Esteban Ocon’s confirmation that he will leave the American outfit at the end of this season, whilst fellow Ferrari-backed driver Bearman is likely to retain his seat.

title: How a chat with Prost inspired Wolff's F1 driver management
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has revealed that a conversation with Alain Prost early in his own Formula 1 career inspired the Mercedes Team Principal in how to deal with fractious relationships between his drivers.

Under Wolff's leadership, Mercedes has secured a plethora of titles and victories, notably with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg as the Silver Arrows dominated F1 in the mid-2010s.

But this came at a cost, with Wolff having to deal with several flashpoints following on-track collisions in one of the sport's most heated rivalries.

Speaking after last weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, Wolff recalled a conversation he had with four-time World Champion Prost, who had his own legendary rivalry with McLaren team mate Ayrton Senna that resulted in a long-lasting feud even after they raced for separate teams.

"It was very early in my Formula 1 life, I was at Williams, and I remember, as [if] it was yesterday, I was on the grid, and I think he [Prost] was involved in Renault back in the day or something," said Wolff.

"I said to him, I saw it on TV, the whole thing, and how did that escalate between the two of you, almost in a naive way because I didn't understand the dynamics between the drivers, and he said the problem was that you never knew whether you were favoured.

"He said at times I felt that, it was me, it was Alain that was the one that was favoured and then at different stages of the years, it was Ayrton.

"He said that created a dynamic of mistrust in the team and you felt that your direct opponent may be given advantages. Even if it's just emotional at the end the drivers are little traumatised eight-year-olds that were put in a go-kart, they were scared, it was a parent's dream that they were chasing.

"Eventually you end up in Formula 1 and they tell you, now you have to be, you have to play the team game and it's Mercedes or it's McLaren, so it's very difficult."

While not as severe as the Hamilton/Rosberg dynamic, Wolff has had to step in between his current drivers this season, noticeably in Canada when Kimi Antonelli and George Russell went wheel-to-wheel.

But the Austrian believes a transparent and open approach in how the team deals with such issues has made Mercedes stronger, with both Antonelli and Russell obeying team orders this season to help the other driver despite being in a battle for the title.

"You need to feel emotionally protected by the team and I think if you don't do that and you keep it transparent and balanced, that can create moments where the driver just loses confidence and from that learning for me was, okay, I can never do that," he said.

"I need to be transparent, and if one day we decide to play the team game in whatever form, I will say so. I will be saying, these are the rules now, and we'll be very open and transparent.

"And if we have a discussion because the driver disagrees or someone in the team says we should do it differently, then fine, let's have the discussion. So, I would think that this is how we want to behave."

title: Mekies signs long-term contract extension with Red Bull

title: Freddie Hunt on father James’ legacy 50 years after his title
excerpt:
Freddie Hunt has been reflecting on his father James' title triumph half a century on from the Briton's success and how the iconic driver "glamorised the sport".

It has been 50 years since James Hunt claimed the 1976 Formula 1 World Championship, beating Niki Lauda by just one point in one of the most dramatic title battles in the sport’s history.

The British driver’s triumph came at the season finale in Japan – the exact anniversary falls on the Saturday of the United States GP weekend in Austin – with his rivalry against Lauda and his larger-than-life personality making him one of F1's most memorable and beloved figures.

Speaking on the latest episode of official F1 podcast Beyond The Grid, Hunt’s son Freddie reflected on the anniversary and what made his father such a formidable competitor.

“Fifty years is an awfully long time ago, it’s amazing how the sport has evolved since then,” said Freddie.

“1976 was one of the most incredible seasons in the history of Formula 1. I think that whole era of racing was one of the best.”

Opening up about his father’s greatest strength, Freddie believes it was his ability to adapt, even when his car wasn’t performing as expected.

“I think even when the set-up wasn’t great, he managed to drive around problems,” he explained.

“The first Formula 1 race he won, [the BRDC International Trophy] at Silverstone, the knob on the gearstick broke off, so he did half the race with the spike digging into his hand.

“And then the British Grand Prix in ‘76, because of the hastily-repaired car after the first-lap incident, they didn’t have the set-up right at all. They didn’t have time to.

“He said in the interview afterwards it was understeering an awful lot to begin with, but then it gradually got better. I think he just managed to figure out how to adapt his driving to still go quickly with a wonky car.”

Arguably as famous as his adaptability was Hunt’s fierce rivalry with Lauda, which became immortalised on the silver screen in the 2013 hit film Rush, starring Chris Hemsworth as Hunt and Daniel Brühl as Lauda.

But despite their competitiveness on track, Hunt and Lauda shared a close friendship away from racing, with Freddie recalling an amusing story the Austrian driver once told him.

“They’re opposites, and opposites often attract," Freddie said. "I think they shared the same sense of humour and they were good mates.

“They were testing one day and they had the track. Niki said, ‘James, I’m flying down. If you want a lift in the plane, you’re welcome to, but make sure you’re not late.'

“I think Niki was literally on the runway, revving up the engines, about to take off, and Dad arrives. I think he was a little bit hungover, gets on the plane, puts his music on and has a nap.

50 years since the iconic season that inspired 'Rush'

“Off they go testing, and Dad didn’t come back round. So everyone panics, thinking he’d had a shunt. He’d set some quick lap times, got bored of testing, basically pulled over and had a nap. I don’t think Niki was very impressed!”

Their friendship was particularly evident following Lauda’s near-fatal accident at the Nurburgring in 1976, with Hunt regularly contacting his rival as he recovered in hospital.

“Dad wanted to race against him," Freddie explained. "He wrote to him saying, ‘Get better soon because I need to race against you.'

“He was phoning him every day in hospital and writing to him, cheering him on. ‘Hurry up, get ready, come back quick.'”

Lauda made a remarkable return to racing at the Italian Grand Prix just 42 days after his accident, missing only two Grands Prix. This was despite still recovering from severe burns to his face and head.

Wearing bandages beneath his helmet caused considerable pain given his injuries but the Austrian battled through to finish fourth at Monza. Lauda’s extraordinary comeback kept the championship fight alive, with Hunt eventually securing the title by a single point at the rain-soaked Japanese Grand Prix.

“Dad said he wished they could have shared the championship," Freddie admitted. "They both deserved to win it.”

Beyond his achievements on track, Hunt’s personality helped bring a new level of glitz and glamour to Formula 1, with his influence still felt half a century later.

Reflecting on his father’s legacy, Freddie expressed his pride in how Hunt continues to be remembered.

“He glamorised the sport," Freddie said. "He had a significant impact on F1, I think, and on sport in general. He’s well remembered and it’s lovely. I’m always hearing new stories from people.

“I’m tremendously proud of him. What he did, what he achieved and how he achieved it with humility and integrity. He was much loved.”

title: The 27 tracks Verstappen has won at after Singapore triumph
excerpt:
Max Verstappen triumphed in Singapore with Red Bull at the weekend, to take his maiden Grand Prix victory at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

The Dutchman won on his 10th attempt under the lights of F1’s original night race to round off an incredible weekend for the four-time World Champion, which also included victory in the Sprint too.

Singapore has long been something of a ‘bogey’ track for Verstappen, despite four previous front row starts and four podiums. His nine starts there without a win was the highest of any current venue on the F1 calendar – but he has finally put that stat to bed with a victory that looked assured from the second he made it to Turn 1 ahead of Charles Leclerc.

Verstappen’s win means he has now tasted victory at 27 different F1 circuits, second only to Lewis Hamilton’s 31. So, where has the Dutchman won, and which are his most successful circuits?

The Red Bull Ring – Austria

Red Bull always seem to go well on home soil and, until Zandvoort joined the calendar, Spielberg was Verstappen’s de facto home race. The orange-clad Dutch fans used to cross the border to Austria in their thousands to cheer him on, and Verstappen more often than not made their journey worthwhile.

He first won there back in 2018, followed that up with another victory in 2019, and then won twice in 2021 when the circuit hosted back-to-back events during the pandemic. His last victory at the Red Bull Ring was a win from pole in 2023, that result coming in the midst of an incredible run of 10 straight victories as he galloped that year to a third straight title.

Poles: 5

The Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez - Mexico City

The race in Mexico City is run at high altitude, which often worked well for the Red Bull aero package. As such, Verstappen won back-to-back races in 2017 and 2018 despite his car not being the class of the field across those two seasons.

Verstappen only won two races in 2017 and two in 2018, making it all the more remarkable that victories in Mexico City featured in both seasons.

Three victories in three of his Championship-winning years of 2021, 2022 and 2023 followed, but only one of those was from pole, which makes his results all the more incredible. He was able to share the podium with Mexican team mate Sergio Perez in 2021 and 2022 too, which given the top three park up in the stadium section at the end of the race, must have been quite the atmosphere to experience.

Wins: 5

Poles: 1

Yas Marina Circuit – Abu Dhabi

Yas Marina traditionally hosts the final race of the season, and while some drivers have already taken their foot off the gas and have half a mind on Christmas, Verstappen always turns up with his game face on.

He won in Abu Dhabi four years running between 2020 and 2023, all of those victories coming from pole. His win in 2020 helped springboard his Championship charge in 2021, while his next two wins came at the end of dominant seasons.

He also won from pole there last season, which was not quite enough to clinch the title with Lando Norris’ third place finish enough for the McLaren man to seal the crown. Nonetheless, it is a track Verstappen tends to go well at – not that there are many he doesn’t these days.

Wins: 5

Poles: 5

Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya – Spain

Barcelona was where Verstappen got his first taste of what it felt like to win in F1, in his debut race for Red Bull no less. Having been promoted from Toro Rosso mid-season, he benefitted from the two Mercedes cars colliding at the start and went on to take a famous win at the age of just 18. That made him the youngest-ever winner in F1, a record that still stands today.

He also won in three of his Championship years in 2022, 2023 and 2024, but only once from pole. The other two wins came from second on the grid though, so he is no slouch over one lap in the often scorching hot conditions of Barcelona.

Wins: 4

Poles: 1

Circuit of The Americas - USA

Verstappen has won four out of the last five Grands Prix in Texas, taking victory in 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025. The first and last of those came from pole, which is not always an advantage in Austin given the long uphill run to Turn 1 that allows for so many different racing lines.

His win in 2023 came from sixth on the grid, the Dutchman made to work hard for the victory after brake issues emerged mid-race. That was his 50th career Grand prix win, a number that has since been dwarfed – his current tally is 73 wins, all with one constructor.

Wins: 4

Poles: 2

Suzuka - Japan

Suzuka is one of those tracks everyone wants to win at and is often cited as the best to drive on the calendar with its sweeping, high-speed corners. Verstappen has won four times in Japan, those victories coming between 2022 and 2025.

His first win was in the wet too, Verstappen giving one of his masterclasses to take not just the victory but also the World Championship crown at one of the most famous venues in motorsport.

The Dutchman’s results have all been built from strong qualifying performances, Verstappen taking all of those victories from pole. He could not make it five from five this season, Red Bull not starting 2026 as strongly as they would have hoped.

Wins: 4

Poles: 4

Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari (Imola) - Italy

Verstappen’s record at Imola is truly spectacular. The circuit returned to the calendar in 2020, stepping in as the schedule chopped and changed due to the pandemic. Verstappen might have failed to finish the first race in cold November conditions, but he then won the four subsequent editions.

A win rate of 80% at a track is not to be sniffed at, with two of those victories coming from pole too.

Wins: 4

Poles: 2

Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace (Interlagos) – Brazil

One of Verstappen’s most famous Brazil drives was not for the win, the Dutchman scything his way through the field in treacherous, wet conditions back in 2016 to bag a podium. But he has taken victory at Interlagos three times, from pole in 2019 and 2023, and then from P17 on the grid in 2024.

That last win was another masterclass from the Dutchman in wet conditions, as he survived red flags and plenty of chaos to not just climb back through the field, but win by nearly 20 seconds in an imperious display of car mastery.

Wins: 3

Poles: 2

Lusail International Circuit – Qatar

One of the newer editions to the calendar, Qatar has hosted four Grands Prix so far, in 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025. Verstappen has won three of them for a 75% success rate, buoyed by often having the best car towards the end of the season, such are Red Bull’s development strengths.

He has only taken pole once, back in 2023 when he beat George Russell over one lap by nearly half a second. Last year, the Dutchman won from third on the grid with Red Bull nailing their strategy calls to help Verstappen beat the McLaren pair, which at the time ensured the Championship fight would go to the last race of the season.

Wins: 3

Poles: 1

Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve – Canada

Montreal is another circuit that can throw up chaotic races, not to mention the Wall of Champions that has caught many a famous driver out over the years.

Two of Verstappen’s three wins have come from pole in 2022 and 2023, the other in 2024 coming from second on the grid. He also has three other podiums here, and yes, he has hit the famous wall back in 2024, fortunately doing so in practice.

Wins: 3

Poles: 2

Autodromo Nazionale Monza - Italy

The Temple of Speed rewards cars that have good low-drag set-ups, something Red Bull have not always necessarily had as a strength. But Verstappen still has three victories at a track where speed is everything, winning in 2022 and 2023, before grabbing victory from pole in 2025.

This was not his best track in his early career, the Dutchman failing to finish on the podium in his first seven outings here, with reliability woes also not aiding his cause. But a win from seventh on the grid in 2022 changed that, Verstappen beating Leclerc as he finally got to stand on the top step of one of the most impressive podiums in the sport.

Wins: 3

Poles: 2

Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps - Belgium

Spa is another home race for Verstappen, and not just because so many Dutch fans can make their way to the Ardennes Forest relatively easily. His mother is Belgian, although Verstappen races under the Dutch flag like his father.

Like Suzuka, Spa is one of those historic tracks everyone wants to win at, with Verstappen doing so for three consecutive years from 2021. His 2022 win was from 14th on the grid, the Dutchman’s car the class of the field as he made light work of recovering from grid penalties in one of his title-winning years.

Wins: 3

Poles: 1

Circuit Zandvoort – The Netherlands

Zandvoort joined the calendar in 2021, with Verstappen winning the first three editions of his home race. All of those wins were from pole too, the Dutch fans not minding his dominance one bit as they enjoyed watching their man do what he does best.

Verstappen followed those wins up with two second-place finishes, but sadly his final Dutch Grand Prix saw him crash out early after dipping a wheel onto the slippery white lines following some earlier rain.

Wins: 3

Poles: 3

Jeddah Corniche Circuit – Saudi Arabia

Another relative newcomer on the calendar, Jeddah is a fast, exhilarating street track that has caught out more than one driver since its first race in 2021. But thus far, Verstappen’s record there is fairly eye-catching, with two wins and three second-place finishes from the five editions so far.

While he has two poles at the track as well, his best result is arguably his P2 in 2023, achieved from 15th on the grid after a driveshaft failure cost him in Qualifying. The issue returned late on in the race, leaving the Dutchman no chance to try and challenge Perez ahead for the win.

Wins: 2

Poles: 2

Sepang International Circuit – Malaysia

Verstappen was the last driver to win in Malaysia back in 2017, the circuit then dropping off the calendar. But it reappeared in 2026 as host of the Bahrain Grand Prix, and the Dutchman picked up where he left off.

He won from third on the grid in 2017 for what was then just his second-ever F1 victory, but in 2026 the four-time World Champion put an at times difficult season to bed with his first win of the year, from pole no less.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Las Vegas Strip Circuit – USA

Verstappen won the inaugural Las Vegas Grand Prix in 2023, having to work hard for the win after picking up a time penalty in a slightly chaotic race that saw several Safety Car periods, the Dutchman overtaking Perez and Charles Leclerc late on to take the victory.

He won again last year as part of his late charge to the title – which ultimately saw him come up just short in Abu Dhabi.

Wins: 2

Poles: 0

Baku City Circuit – Azerbaijan

Baku has not always been a happy hunting ground for Verstappen, who has had a few brushes with the walls over the years here. He crashed out when leading in 2021 thanks to a tyre issue, while 2018 will long be remembered for a collision between Verstappen and his team mate at the time, Daniel Ricciardo.

But Verstappen does have two wins at the street track, winning in 2022 before taking victory from pole in 2025. He came agonisingly close to a third victory this season, just unable to out-drag Russell’s Mercedes across the line.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Hungaroring – Hungary

The Hungaroring near Budapest is reminiscent of a karting track and is another one the drivers love, but it lends itself to a very specific car set-up, and is somewhere Red Bull have not always excelled. Verstappen recorded back-to-back victories in 2022 and 2023, but has not won there since while his only pole was back in 2019.

His win in 2022 is the highlight, Red Bull nailing their strategy as Verstappen recovered from P10 on the grid, pulling off multiple overtakes and even surviving a late spin to beat Lewis Hamilton and Russell.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Miami International Autodrome – USA

Miami joined the calendar in 2022, with Verstappen taking the inaugural win. He followed that up with victory in 2023 too, but since then things have not gone entirely to plan in the Sunshine State.

Poles in 2024 and 2025 did not yield victory, while this season Verstappen trailed home in fifth-place in a car that Red Bull were still fighting to understand.

Wins: 2

Poles: 2

Circuit de Monaco - Monaco

Verstappen’s first Monaco victory came in 2021 from second on the grid – but with pole-sitter Leclerc unable to take the start, the Dutchman was de facto P1. He won from pole in 2023 as well, but this street track has not always been his forte.

He has only started from the front row three times at a circuit where grid slots are everything, while this season, anti-stall cost him off the line before he was forced into retirement with more mechanical woes.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Bahrain International Circuit - Bahrain

Verstappen’s two wins in Bahrain came in 2023 and 2024, when his Red Bull was the class of the field. Both years Bahrain was hosting the opening race too, meaning Verstappen’s season got off to the best possible start.

He also has three poles at the desert track, along with two other podiums. And the record books will state he has won three Bahrain Grands Prix, having taken victory in Malaysia this season which was hosting on behalf of Bahrain.

Wins: 2

Poles: 3

Silverstone – Great Britain

Given how often Silverstone throws up some questionable weather, it might be something of a surprise that Verstappen has not won more than twice in Northamptonshire. His first victory was the 70th Anniversary Grand Prix in 2020, and he won again in 2023.

That second victory came from pole, while the two other times he started P1 did not go so well – an infamous collision with Hamilton ending his race early in 2021, while he trailed home fifth in 2025 despite the race being held in those wet-dry conditions he normally favours.

Wins: 2

Poles: 3

Circuit Paul Ricard – France

France last hosted a Grand Prix in 2022, with Verstappen winning that edition from pole position. He has raced at Paul Ricard four times, winning in 2021 as well, while 2018 yielded a podium and 2019 saw him come home in fourth-place.

Wins: 2

Poles: 1

Albert Park – Australia

Melbourne has not always been kind to Verstappen, the Dutchman failing to finish three times at Albert Park with mechanical gremlins. But he has won there just the once, back in 2023 when he took victory from pole.

He also started on pole in 2024, but brake issues did for his race that season.

Wins: 1

Poles: 2

Shanghai International Circuit – China

Verstappen only has two podiums in China from eight attempts, one of those a victory back in 2024 from pole. His record might have been improved had Shanghai hosted a race during some of Red Bull’s dominant years, the circuit not featuring on the calendar for four years from 2020.

Wins: 1

Poles: 1

Hockenheim – Germany

Verstappen won the last German Grand Prix to be held back in 2019, a humdinger of a race that saw the Dutchman pit five times in rainy conditions, yo-yoing his way from the back to the front as Red Bull excelled with their strategy calls – helped no end by Verstappen’s input from the cockpit.

On a day where many drivers were left looking a little foolish in tricky conditions, Verstappen again underlined why he was rated so highly, something that has not changed in the subsequent years.

Wins: 1

Poles: 0

Marina Bay Street Circuit - Singapore

Finally, the one that got away so many times but not in 2026. Singapore throws up some of the hottest, most humid conditions of the season, which has not always favoured Red Bull. The team won three times with Sebastian Vettel, while Perez also took a win under the lights at Marina Bay.

But finally in 2026, Verstappen had the car, the speed in Qualifying, made no mistakes and was able to tick off a new track, having now stood on the top step of the rostrum at 27 different venues.

Wins: 1

Poles: 1

Could Verstappen add to his tally in 2027?

There are three venues on the calendar for next season Verstappen has not yet won at – Portimao in Portugal, the Madring in Spain and Istanbul Park in Turkey.

Verstappen has raced at all three, with second-place in Turkey his best result from two efforts, while he bagged two podiums in two attempts at Portimao.

The Madring joined the calendar for the first time this season, with the Dutchman finishing second to Kimi Antonelli.

title: 'We owe him one' – Mekies on Hadjar's Singapore issues
excerpt:
For Isack Hadjar, the Singapore Grand Prix weekend proved to be one to forget after a nightmare series of technical issues impacted almost every track session.

Even on race day things didn’t go perfectly to plan, but he was at least able to put in a storming charge from the pit lane to finish 10th.

After the race Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies was quick to apologise for the problems that denied Hadjar the chance to show what he could do, noting that “we owe him one”.

Hadjar arrived at the final race of the triple header on the back of his superb drive to third in Azerbaijan, and frustration in Malaysia after a late power unit glitch saw him lose another potential P3 as he slipped back to fifth.

In Singapore things started to go wrong in Friday’s Sprint Qualifying as he again had PU issues, and had to settle for P9.

“What seemed like a good start of the day turned into really very poor performance,” he said. “I never got to have a good lap really, I'm just fighting with the car, had engine issues on the last run. Just struggling. I don't know, it's just weird.”

Saturday proved to be even worse when he suffered a PU failure on the third lap of the Sprint. A great effort from the RBR crew saw him switch to previously used elements for Qualifying.

However, from the start of the session he suffered a gearbox issue – the result of a perfect storm of events going wrong – and having lost fourth gear he was not able to do a flying lap. To add insult to injury, after he parked up the car was doused with extinguishant.

“Today was a disaster,” he rued. “I could have stayed back in Paris, and it would have been the same…”

The team was left with a lot of work to do, and it was decided to break parc ferme, add a new power unit to the pool, and start from the pit lane.

At the start he lost out initially to fellow pit lane starter Fernando Alonso as once again PU issues struck, but thereafter he found the pace to move up the field. He eventually made it to P10, finishing just 6s behind George Russell, who had started from 19th on the grid.

“It was good for everything that's happened,” Hadjar said after the flag. “Definitely good pace, but I don't know what to say. It's just surprising we could make that race entertaining, considering it's very difficult to overtake around that track. I'm quite happy about that. But I would have liked to make use of that pace to fight for a win.

“I just sent it, but at some point I thought this is a train, I'm never going to finish in the top 10. And then on that soft tyre, I knew I had good pace to unlock, but I didn't think I would be that fast. So that was nice.”

To his credit, he was keen to praise his crew for their hard work: “It was challenging for my mechanics. They suffered quite a lot for just one point. So it's definitely their weekend, and they deserve better. So we try again.”

Mekies stressed that the team had let Hadjar down with the reliability issues.

“We had a pretty horrific weekend on his side of the garage,” said the Frenchman. “We basically didn't give him any chance to do any competitive laps before the main race on Sunday.

“We had a number of different mechanical issues – some on the PU, some on the gearbox, some other glitches. So it was really like a nightmare weekend.

“In that context, the crew – not only Isack's crew, but it also was fully involving Max [Verstappen]'s crew who helped – the other side of the garage was under the car changing massive components all weekend long up to this morning in parc ferme before the race start, which is probably not what you want on the last of three in a triple header in hot and humid weather.

“So huge, massive congrats to the to the crew for what they've done. I've never seen such an incredible turnaround, and to then deliver a faultless race car on Sunday. Nonetheless, we have lost the chance to see Isack's speed here. So we owe him one.”

Mekies was impressed with what Hadjar was able to achieve despite the problems: “In the race, starting last and spending 90% of the race in traffic, he still showed very, very strong pace, which only confirmed that he would probably have been up there on the sharp end of the classification.

“So it's on us. But he certainly has shown that he had the speed with a few laps he done on Sunday.”

Verstappen’s domination of the Singapore weekend with two poles and two wins indicated just how competitive the RB22 is at the moment, and Hadjar is keen to bounce back with a clean weekend at the US GP.

“Now since Malaysia, I'm just desperate to have a car that's working a bit better on my side to fight for a win,” he said. “Because at the moment, it's not possible to fight. So now we need to reset, understand what happened since Sunday in Malaysia, and make sure to come back in Austin and fight for podiums.”

title: Christian Horner clarifies Ferrari 'dream job' remark as F1 return wait continues
excerpt:
Those comments made headlines, and now the former Red Bull boss has moved to clear the air.

Christian Horner has moved to clarify his recent remarks about Ferrari.

Horner has insisted that a comment describing the Maranello outfit as a "dream job" was taken out of context and that any return to Formula 1 would hinge on securing an ownership stake rather than a straightforward hiring.

The former Red Bull boss left the Milton Keynes-based team in 2025 under a formal severance agreement reported to be worth around £80 million, concluding a contract that had been scheduled to run through 2030.

Terms of that exit are understood to have reduced his overall payout in exchange for a shorter non-compete period, clearing the way for Horner to explore F1 opportunities again from early 2026.

Since then, Horner has been linked to investor consortia rather than conventional team principal vacancies, including a confirmed approach as part of a group exploring Otro Capital's 24 per cent minority stake in Alpine.

Ferrari, however, operates as an internal racing division of Ferrari N.V., not a separate sellable franchise, meaning no outside party can buy equity in the Scuderia alone.

[Article continues below]

Horner - Ferrary aren't going to sell shares

Speaking to The Guardian, Horner was careful to praise Fred Vasseur, who signed a multi-year contract extension with Ferrari in July 2025 and has since been publicly backed by senior Ferrari executives John Elkann and Benedetto Vigna amid paddock chatter over his long-term position.

"Fred Vasseur is an experienced guy," Horner said. "He's done a decent job. But I, more than anyone, know the pressures of running a competitive organisation. My comments got taken out of context.

"Ferrari is the biggest brand in F1. It's the most historic team. But I've accumulated some phenomenal capital behind me, to look at the next move I potentially make in the sport.

"That would be with ownership attached to it, and Ferrari aren't going to sell shares.

"So I'm happy to sit outside the sport and see what opportunities present themselves over the coming months or years.

"It's not a prerequisite that I go back. I would only return for the right opportunity with like-minded people that want to win. I would never go back just to take part."

Horner's comments confirm he is pursuing an equity-linked route back into the sport, having built financial backing that he has described as giving him leverage to wait for the right project rather than accept any available seat on the pit wall.

title: Liam Lawson opens door to major motorsport event: 'Something I'd love to do'
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has opened the door to competing at the Race of Champions when the event lands in his home country in January.

The Race of Champions, an annual end-of-season head-to-head that pits drivers from across motorsport against one another in identical machinery, is set to take place in Wellington, giving the country's fans a rare chance to watch their own compete on home soil.

Racing Bulls driver Lawson, though, was careful not to get ahead of himself when asked about his involvement. "I'm not actually sure yet," he said, speaking to media, including RacingNews365.

"But it looks like something that'll be really, really cool. I should be there over at that time as well, so yeah, it'd be something I'd love to do."

For a driver who has spent his career racing on the other side of the world, a January event in Wellington would mean lining up in front of a home crowd rather than a television audience, so the appeal is obvious.

The Race of Champions is built on exactly that kind of occasion: a compact, knockout format that throws drivers from different disciplines into the same car and lets the result settle any argument.

For New Zealand, hosting it is a statement in itself as it is a chance to put the country at the centre of the motorsport calendar for a weekend, rather than at the end of a long-haul flight.

Whether Lawson is on the entry list remains to be seen, however, it is clearly an opportunity he is unlikely to refuse if offered.

title: F2 provide clear calendar update despite F1 Middle East finale still at risk
excerpt:
Formula 2 CEO Bruno Michel is confident F1 will head to Qatar and Abu Dhabi to end the current season, meaning the support championship will also reach its planned conclusion.

The ongoing uncertainty in the Middle East, which has already affected the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Grands Prix, means there is still the lingering risk that F1 cannot travel to the region in late November for the final two rounds of the campaign.

Originally planned for April, the weekend in Bahrain was rescheduled for October and relocated to the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia — which F2 did not travel to after replacement rounds in Miami and Montreal — and the event in Jeddah was cancelled altogether.

Linked to the United States-Iran War, it is current insecurity in Saudi Arabia — with Yemeni Houthis launching strikes in the country — that poses the greatest threat.

But the situation remains fluid, and despite a final call from F1 expected in mid-October, further changes cannot be entirely ruled out.

"Well, for the moment, and I think it's completely clear, Qatar and Abu Dhabi are on the calendar, and we are going to finish the championship in Qatar and in Abu Dhabi," Michel told media, including RacingNews365.

"We're following Formula 1 on that. Formula 1 is completely aware of the situation and what needs to be done to make sure that we exercise those two races in the best conditions, which will be the case.

"So we are really looking forward [to it], since we have a fantastic championship to finish with a lot of drivers, three drivers fighting for the title. We're really looking forward to having those two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi."

Could there be a replacement round?

F2's most recent round was in Baku, in support of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. After that weekend, newly announced Haas driver Rafael Camara leads Racing Bulls hopeful Nikola Tsolov by seven points, with Alex Dunne a further 11 points back.

A final round in Imola, over what would be the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix weekend in December, is the most likely contingency plan for F1 at this stage, but it remains to be seen if F2 would also head to Italy to close off the title fight in that eventuality.

Asked whether there might be a replacement round, after Colton Herta indicated in Baku that there may or may not be further races, Michel would not be drawn in on that particular element of the matter.

"Well, Qatar and Abu Dhabi will not be cancelled, and, you know, the drivers always have an opinion on a lot of things," he said.

"But I tell you now: we want to finish the season there for sure, and that's what Formula 1 is doing as well, and that's where we're going, too."

title: Lando Norris U-turn defended after 'cocky' Singapore media outburst
excerpt:
Lando Norris' dramatic change of tone after colliding with Oscar Piastri in Singapore has been defended by Guenther Steiner, who insisted the McLaren driver's apology was genuine rather than an exercise in damage control after coming across as "cocky".

Norris clipped Piastri's right-rear tyre while attempting a late lunge at Turn 5 on the final lap of the sprint race, sending his team-mate spinning and out of the session on the spot.

Norris continued to finish eighth, but in the aftermath he refused to accept blame, instead deflecting responsibility in front of the media. The stewards later classed the clash as a racing incident, with no further action taken.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was far from satisfied with that explanation, and reportedly made clear to Norris that the collision between team-mates was unacceptable. B

y the time Sunday's grand prix was done, with Norris finishing fourth and Piastri recovering to fifth, the Briton's position had shifted entirely: he took full responsibility for the crash and even offered support over team radio to help Piastri's recovery drive.

Asked whether that turnaround was sincere or simply an attempt to smooth things over, Steiner told the Red Flags podcast that he could understand the scepticism, but believed Stella's intervention had been decisive.

"That is now difficult to look into," began Steiner. "I think he said sorry to everyone except Piastri about it.

"The next day (Sunday), it seemed like, whoa, whoa, whoa! Now you're overdoing it the wrong way. You're a dick one day, and the next day you are the opposite. So I don't know for sure.

"He sat down with Andrea, and I think Andrea, in these situations, is very good. I couldn't be very good. And I think he made him feel like a wanker.

"He just explained to him that this is not happening."

Lando Norris 'realisation' triggered post-grand prix apology

Steiner went further, arguing that Norris had genuinely reflected on his conduct rather than performing a calculated climbdown.

"And I do not think that Lando just did it for, call it a political reason, to make himself, 'Oh, I apologise now, and then I'm alright again.' Actually, he thought about it, and he came to the conclusion that what I did was actually pretty stupid," added Steiner.

"There was no need for it, and especially the reaction afterwards. Because when you do it, when you crash into your team-mate, you shouldn't do it, but it can happen.

"But the reaction from him was not Lando-esque, to say, 'I've got the number one' and all this stuff. This is not him, in my opinion.

"So he realised he was a little bit too cocky about that and needed to go the other way."

title: Rafael Camara joins remarkable and historic F1 legacy of excellence
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has signed for Haas and will be on the F1 grid in 2027. He will become the 34th driver from Brazil to compete. We look back on the country's F1 legacy.

Rafael Camara will become the 34th Brazilian to compete in Formula 1 after Haas agreed to sign the Ferrari junior for 2027, replacing Esteban Ocon alongside Oliver Bearman.

The deal is understood to have been finalised during the recent Singapore Grand Prix weekend, with Haas and Ferrari reaching agreement on terms that will put Camara on the grid next year.

The 21-year-old also arrives with backing from Brazilian state transport and logistics firm Transpetro, commercial support that sat alongside his Ferrari ties in Haas's decision-making.

He now adds to Brazil's long legacy in Formula 1 that began in the 1950s with Chico Landi, who became the country's first starter in the championship, taking six race entries across stints with Ferrari and Maserati between 1951 and 1956.

Since then, 32 Brazilians have followed him onto an F1 grid, from early pioneers such as Gino Bianco and Hermano da Silva Ramos through to more recent names like Pietro Fittipaldi and Gabriel Bortoleto.

The country's golden eras came through Emerson Fittipaldi, Nelson Piquet and Ayrton Senna, who combined for eight F1 drivers' championships between them across three decades.

Fittipaldi won with Lotus and McLaren; Piquet took titles with Brabham and Williams, whilst Senna built his legacy with three championships at McLaren.

[Article continues below]

© XPBImages

Brazil's glory years

The generation that followed kept Brazil firmly on the grid even without matching those championship exploits.

Rubens Barrichello spent years as Michael Schumacher's team-mate at Ferrari during the team's dominant run from 2000 to 2004, finishing as championship runner-up twice before later fighting for the title again with Brawn GP in 2009.

Felipe Massa came within a single point of the drivers' championship in 2008, losing out to Lewis Hamilton at Interlagos, and remained a mainstay for Ferrari and then Williams until his retirement after 2017.

Nelson Piquet Jr. had a shorter and more turbulent spell in the sport, his time at Renault remembered chiefly for the fallout from the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix, when he was ordered to crash deliberately to trigger a safety car that helped Fernando Alonso to victory.

Alongside them, drivers including Pedro Diniz, Ricardo Zonta, Cristiano da Matta, Antonio Pizzonia, Bruno Senna and Felipe Nasr, all added grand prix starts and occasional points for midfield and customer teams between the 1990s and 2010s.

Following Massa's retirement at the end of 2017, Brazil then went without a full-time representative, a gap broken only by Pietro Fittipaldi's stand-in appearances in 2020, before Bortoleto's arrival restored the country's regular presence on the grid.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

Brazilian decline and revival

The decline in Brazilian representation during this period has been attributed to the rising cost of climbing Europe's junior single-seater ladder, worsened by unfavourable exchange rates and the retreat of domestic sponsorship money once the tobacco-advertising era, built around backers such as Marlboro and Souza Cruz, came to an end, with Petrobras also scaling back its driver programmes.

Earlier Brazilian regional junior championships, including Formula Chevrolet and Formula 3 Sudamericana, also collapsed as car counts shrank and costs rose, culminating in the demise of the revived Formula 3 Brasil championship at the end of 2017 and leaving young karting graduates with no domestic stepping stone before they had to relocate to Europe, often at a very young age.

Brazil's motorsport authorities moved to address that gap in 2022 with the launch of the FIA-certified F4 Brazilian Championship, run by Vicar and the CBA, giving karting graduates a nationally based route that carries FIA Super Licence points before a move abroad.

Bortoleto, now racing for Audi after his rookie season with Sauber, is the most visible product of the renewed pipeline, having progressed through management agency A14 and the McLaren junior programme before reaching the grid.

His case, alongside that of Camara, has coincided with a broader revival in Brazilian corporate backing for motorsport, with domestic investment banks and technology firms increasingly funding drivers as they target international exposure.

Once he lines up on the grid, Camara will join Bortoleto as the second Brazilian driver on the 2027 grid, the first time the country has had multiple representatives in Formula 1 in well over a decade.

title: Who is Rafael Camara? The low down on new Haas driver for 2027
excerpt:
Haas has confirmed Rafael Camara as its second driver for 2027, ending Esteban Ocon's two-year spell with the American outfit.

The 21-year-old Brazilian, a Ferrari Driver Academy product since 2021, will line up alongside Oliver Bearman at the Banbury-based team from next season.

Camara joins after working his way through the junior single-seater ladder with remarkable consistency, culminating in back-to-back titles that have made him one of the grid's most highly rated prospects.

Camara was born in Recife and built his reputation in karting, winning the WSK Champions Cup, WSK Super Master Series and Champions of the Future titles in 2021. That form earned him a place at Ferrari's World Scouting Finals and, from there, a route into the Ferrari Driver Academy.

His car racing career began in 2022 with Prema Racing, where he finished runner-up in Formula 4 UAE and third overall in both Italian F4 and ADAC Formula 4 in his rookie single-seater campaign.

[Article continues below]

The road to Formula 3 and F2 for Camara

Camara moved into Formula Regional for 2023 and 2024, finishing third in the Middle East Championship in both years before claiming the 2024 FRECA title with a round to spare, taking seven wins along the way.

Stepping up to FIA Formula 3 with Trident in 2025, he won the championship as a rookie, taking four feature race victories and becoming the team's third consecutive F3 champion after Gabriel Bortoleto and Leonardo Fornaroli.

For this year, Camara graduated to Formula 2 with Invicta Racing. He has won at Barcelona, Spa-Francorchamps and Baku to lead the standings with two rounds to spare in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, providing they go ahead given the continuing uncertainty in the region due to the Iran-US war.

His sporting credentials for a Super Licence were effectively locked in once he won FRECA and F3 in consecutive seasons, comfortably clearing the mandatory 40-point threshold.

He has also already sampled contemporary F1 machinery, completing a Testing of Previous Cars outing in a Ferrari SF-25 at the Hungaroring in May, with further TPC mileage in Haas machinery following over the summer.

Haas confirmed at the end of September that Ocon would leave at season's end, after falling short of internal expectations alongside Bearman. For Camara, the step up caps a rapid rise through the junior categories.

title: Williams make early announcement for special name of 2027 F1 car
excerpt:
Williams will mark its 50th anniversary in 2027 by naming next year's challenger the FW50, skipping the usual chassis numbering to honour half a century in Formula 1.

The Grove-based squad's new car would ordinarily have carried the FW49 designation, following this year's FW48. But Williams has opted to jump straight to FW50, mirroring the leap it made from FW38 to FW40 for its 40th anniversary season.

A show car of the FW50 will form part of a wider calendar of celebrations announced by the team, with fans placed "at the heart of the action" throughout the milestone year.

The centrepiece of the anniversary will be 'W50 Live', a ticketed event open to the public from 11-28 February in Waterloo, London.

The multi-sensory exhibition will take fans through five decades of Williams history, featuring championship-winning cars and some of the team's most iconic memorabilia.

The choice of venue carries symbolic weight. Just over 50 years after founder Frank Williams discovered co-founder Patrick Head working in a garage under a London railway arch, the team will celebrate its legacy beneath the capital's railway arches again.

That legacy spans nine constructors' championships, seven drivers' titles and 114 Grand Prix victories.

[Article continues below]

100 teams in F1 have come and gone since Williams started racing

On display at the event will be the FW06, the first car built by Williams Grand Prix Engineering, alongside the FW11B that carried Nelson Piquet to the title in 1987 and the dominant FW14B that secured Nigel Mansell's championship in 1992.

Also featured will be the FW19, marking 30 years since Jacques Villeneuve's 1997 title win; the FW25 which set an F1 average speed record under Juan Pablo Montoya that stood for 17 years; and the FW38, which still holds the record for the highest speed ever reached by an F1 car, 378kph, set by Valtteri Bottas.

Williams' driver line-up for 2027 has already been confirmed, with Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz partnering for a third successive year.

Albon holds the record for the most F1 starts in Williams history, having surpassed Mansell's previous mark of 95 in Barcelona this year. Sainz, meanwhile, is one of only three drivers, alongside Mansell and Alain Prost, to have raced for Ferrari, McLaren and Williams, the only three teams to reach a 50th anniversary on the grid.

Later in the season, fans will get the chance to vote on a one-off livery for Williams' home race of the British GP at Silverstone.

To mark the anniversary, Williams will also release a series of limited-edition merchandise and collectables celebrating standout moments, personalities and car designs from its history.

These include a W50-branded Monopoly set due on sale before Christmas, and a coffee table book charting 50 years in F1.

Team principal James Vowles said: “It is incredible to think that over 100 F1 teams have come and gone since Frank Williams built this team from next to nothing with a determination to race and win against motorsport’s powerhouses.

"That independence, passion and relentless will to win remain in our DNA as we enter our 50th year.

"Our celebrations will reintroduce the heroes and stories that have forged Williams’ legacy to a new generation of fans, who will carry us forward to reach new heights.”

title: Breaking: Haas sign Ferrari protégé to Formula 1 race seat for 2027
excerpt:
Haas has formally announced the signing of Ferrari's F2 protégé Rafael Camara to an F1 race seat for 2027, as revealed by RacingNews365 last week.

Brazilian Camara, who is 21 years old, will form an all-Ferrari junior line-up at Haas from next season alongside Oliver Bearman, who will be entering his third full-time season with the team.

Frenchman Ocon, who joined ahead of the 2025 season after leaving Alpine, is departing from the squad after two campaigns, with his future uncertain.

Camara, who has sampled Haas F1 machinery during TPC outings, was one of several drivers being evaluated for the seat alongside Bearman, including 2025 FIA F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, a McLaren junior; former Alpine F1 driver and Haas's own third driver, Jack Doohan; and the Toyota-backed Le Mans winner, Ryo Hirakawa.

After the TPC runs, it is understood that the field was narrowed to Camara and Doohan, whose pace had made the choice difficult for owner Gene Haas and team principal Ayao Komatsu.

However, Camara ultimately got the nod to replace Ocon, with RacingNews365 understanding that the decision was taken over the recent Singapore GP weekend, with Camara bringing sizeable sponsorship from Brazil and from the FDA, which he joined in 2022.

He won the 2024 FRECA championship before claiming the 2025 FIA F3 title, beating Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov by 42 points.

In 2026, both Camara and Tsolov stepped up to FIA F2 and are engaged in a fierce battle for the title, with Camara recently overhauling Tsolov and currently leading the standings by seven points.

Camara will join Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto as a full-time Brazilian racer on the grid, the first time two Brazilians will have raced in F1 at the same time since Felipe Massa and Felipe Nasr in 2016.

[Article continues below]

Camara - Time to now focus

Expressing his natural happiness at breaking into F1, Camara said: "It’s an important step in my career, and I want to thank Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me.

"I’m also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey.

"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I’m looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."

title: Lewis Hamilton and Ferrari 'reset' urged after latest strategic shocker
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton had hopes of fighting for victory in Singapore, only to tumble to sixth following a series of shocking strategic decisions.

Lewis Hamilton and Ferrari have been urged to "reset" after another strategic mix-up, this time in Singapore, according to Karun Chandhok, who believes trust between the seven-time champion and his pit wall is "cracking".

The Singapore Grand Prix brought fresh confusion for the Scuderia, with Hamilton finishing sixth after starting in third, well adrift of team-mate Charles Leclerc, who took second behind Max Verstappen.

It came just a week after Ferrari got its tyre call badly wrong in Malaysia, sending Hamilton out on slicks rather than intermediates at the start of a race affected by rain, a decision that left him scrambling to recover while rivals who chose correctly gained large chunks of time.

Chandhok, speaking on the Sky F1 podcast, pointed to contradictory comments from Hamilton in the build-up to the Marina Bay weekend as evidence of friction behind the scenes at Maranello.

Chandhok said: "I think they've got to have some sort of reset because, on Thursday, when we arrived in Singapore, Lewis stood up in the media pen and said, 'I don't understand why Ferrari are being criticised more than anybody else. McLaren also started on the slick tyres. I don't know why we're being criticised more than anybody else.'

"And then, when he was pressed on it, he kind of contradicted himself by saying, 'Well, I of course wanted to start on the intermediates, but I was talked out of it by three other people from the team. We had a meeting and made this decision, and they convinced me to go to the slicks in Malaysia.'"

Lewis Hamilton and Ferrari relationship showing signs of 'cracking'

Hamilton's sixth-place finish in Singapore came as Leclerc banked 18 points to his team-mate's eight, a gap that will do little to ease questions over the communication between the Briton and his side of the Ferrari garage heading into the final rounds of the season.

Singapore was a bizarre race for Hamilton, who apologised to the team as he crossed the finish line and owed up to it being him who chose the unusual strategy and to also not pit during the virtual safety car.

Chandhok went on to argue that the Singapore result compounded the damage, with Hamilton appearing to lose faith in the team's calls on track.

"Already, the trust is slightly cracking, and here (Singapore), he quite clearly decided not to trust their decision," added Chandhok.

"I think he was annoyed by the fact, and I'll rewind it: I think Ferrari played quite a few things badly.

"They started him on the medium tyre, and he was the first to pit. So that straight away is a bit confusing. Of the top seven finishers, he's the only one who started on the medium tyre, and he was the first to pit."

title: McLaren answer vital question after 'doubts' and 'very weird' concern
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella has said the Singapore Grand Prix helped prove that the team had not made the MCL40 slower with its Baku-specification upgrades, having initially had "doubts" on that front.

Andrea Stella has revealed that McLaren feared its Baku upgrade package had made the MCL40 slower, with the team only able to put those doubts to rest after the Singapore Grand Prix.

The Woking-based squad introduced a significant bodywork update at Baku, featuring reworked sidepods and cooling, aimed at boosting straight-line speed around the Azerbaijan circuit's long back straight.

But Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri struggled for pace there and at the following round in Bahrain, leaving the team unable to isolate whether the upgrade itself was to blame.

Matters were not helped by what Stella described as "very weird" data from the Sepang circuit, where unusually rough asphalt disrupted McLaren's usual correlation between trackside readings and its simulation tools.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Stella explained the uncertainty that built up over the two rounds.

"If we take Baku and Malaysia in isolation, we were not very competitive," said the McLaren team principal.

"We had doubts about the package we introduced in Baku; we never expected it to be a big step from a lap-time point of view.

"But because we upgraded two cars at a single time, we had no comparison. We thought, 'Have we made the car slower?'

"At least we were in condition to clarify that that's not the case, which is an important question that we were able to answer in Singapore, going back to a track that is just a little bit more normal than Malaysia, where the track roughness just made the data look very weird. But we understand that it had to do with the track roughness."

[Article continues below]

Baku and Sepang slump

McLaren has endured a sharp downturn compared with last season, when Norris and Piastri regularly fought for wins — and the former won the F1 drivers' title to go with a second successive constructors' crown.

This year the team has had to settle for third in the constructors' standings, 239 points adrift of runaway leaders Mercedes and in danger from Red Bull behind with the gap now just seven points.

That is despite Norris being the class of the field in Hungary, Zandvoort and Madrid, where he won twice and finished third.

Since then McLaren has slipped badly, with Norris ninth at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and fourth in Singapore, while Piastri has not finished higher than fifth across the last four rounds.

Stella pointed to specific technical factors behind the Azerbaijan Grand Prix and Sepang slump.

However, he was pleased that the final leg of the triple-header offered some much-needed clarity.

"And Baku, in which we think that the power unit optimisation played a significant role in terms of lap time," the Italian added.

"We know that this is not only power unit optimisation; there are a few more things on the chassis side that, in the long straights, penalise McLaren in the current configuration, like the [gear] ratios.

"So we had doubts for a couple of races, but we welcome the fact that we were able to clarify that there's nothing wrong going on..."

title: Audi extends long-running partnership into Formula 1 era
excerpt:
Audi has marked a new chapter in its long-running relationship with Öhlins by confirming the suspension specialist as its official supplier.

The Swedish company, which became part of the Brembo Group in January 2025, has been working with Audi on a joint development programme covering engineering, testing and damper performance since before the team's grand prix debut back in March.

That groundwork has now been formalised into an official partnership, coinciding with Audi's first campaign in Formula 1.

The deal is not Öhlins' first involvement with the Ingolstadt manufacturer. Between 1999 and 2016, Audi Sport competed at the 24 Hours of Le Mans using Öhlins dampers across several generations of its sports prototypes, a period that yielded 13 overall victories at the French endurance classic.

Öhlins also supplied dampers for Audi's DTM programme in the 2000s, including for the Audi A4 DTM that was introduced in 2004.

Discussing the new agreement, Öhlins Group Engineering Director Urban Herslöf said the partnership represented a significant point in the company's motorsport history.

"We are proud to partner with Audi Revolut F1 Team in its debut season," said Herslöf.

"For Öhlins, this is a defining moment for our legacy in motorsport, and a powerful platform for us to extend our collaboration with Audi and help shape a new era of automotive performance."
